To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Multiple micronutrient supplementation probably does not reduce mortality in adults living HIV infection.
Multiple micronutrient supplements probably do not reduce the risk of death (low certainty evidence).
Multiple micronutrients probably increase blood levels of vitamin D and may increase blood levels of vitamins A and zinc.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of micronutrient supplementation on mortality and morbidity of HIV-infected adults (not including pregnant women).
the effects of micronutrient supplementation on people living with HIV infection.
the role of micronutritions in the management of HIV.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
There is insufficient evidence to support the use of multiple micronutrient supplements in adults with HIV, and there are no data to support the use in pregnant women with HIV.

the evidence is very low or low quality for most outcomes and that there is no clear evidence of any clinically important effect of multiple micronutrient supplements in adults living with or infected with HIV.

the evidence is very low certainty and there is no effect of multiple or single micronutrient supplementation on mortality in HIV positive adults (including those on ART and those with concurrent active tuberculosis) or on the average of CD4+ cell counts and viral load.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have updated the previous review by including new studies and we have also identified ongoing studies which are likely to change the conclusions.

we have not found evidence to support the routine use of multiple micronutrients for people living with or infected with HIV, but that we do not yet have sufficient data to exclude small beneficial effects.
there is insufficient evidence to determine whether multiple micronutrient supplements have any effect on mortality, disease progression, or HIV related morbidity in HIV positive adults.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the available data do not support routine multiple micronutrients for people living with or at risk of HIV infection in low and middle income settings where micronutrient deficiencies are prevalent.
the current evidence is insufficient to determine whether micronutrient supplementation improves outcomes for HIV positive people in the long term (e.g. mortality).
we found no consistent clinically significant benefit of routine multiple micronutrients supplementation on mortality or morbity in HIV positive adults, including ART naive and ART treated adults.
